title: Teach us to number our days (Psalm 89 [90])
word: Teach us to number our days
hook: a thousand years are as yesterday to God

segments.voice: Yesterday, how lovely are thy tabernacles, and a sparrow at home near the altar. Your line was the sparrow found a home. Today, a psalm about time.

Time is strange. A bad afternoon at the dentist lasts forever. A whole summer vanishes. A photo from ten years ago feels like last month. Next week's calendar is already full. Then comes the moment of looking up and asking: where did it all go? The oldest voice in the whole psalter, by tradition, asked the same thing, and asked God to teach him what to do about it.
screen: `AN AFTERNOON LASTS FOREVER.` → `A SUMMER VANISHES.` → `WHERE DID IT GO?`

segments.voice: Psalm 89 in the Douay, 90 in most Bibles, carries the heading a prayer of Moses, the man of God. It starts with God's time: "Lord, thou hast been our refuge from generation to generation." Before the mountains were born, before the earth was formed, from eternity to eternity, you are God. Then our time: "For a thousand years in thy sight are as yesterday, which is past. And as a watch in the night." A watch was a shift of guard duty, a few hours. A thousand years, to God, is one night shift. The New Testament echoes it: "one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." And human life? Like grass: in the morning it springs up and flowers; by evening it's cut down and dry. Our years are seventy, the psalm says, or eighty if we're strong, and they're gone quickly, and we fly away. It's a hard, honest psalm. Then the line in today's title, the way the Hebrew and the King James have it: teach us to number our days, that we may get a heart of wisdom. Counting the days isn't morbid here. It's the road to a wise heart. A surprise for Douay readers: the old Latin, and the Douay after it, read that verse quite differently, as a prayer that God make his right hand known, and hearts be taught in wisdom. Same hope, different road. The psalm ends asking God to satisfy us in the morning with mercy, and to establish the work of our hands.
screen: `A PRAYER OF MOSES.` · `A THOUSAND YEARS, ONE NIGHT SHIFT.` · `LIKE GRASS BY EVENING.` · `NUMBER OUR DAYS, GET WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Look at the time and work out roughly how many waking hours you have left today: four, nine? Hold that number with attention, not panic, and ask what one thing you'd most want those hours to hold: a conversation, a task, rest, kindness. If you pray, ask as the psalm does, teach me to number my days; if you don't, let the number sharpen what matters.
Teach us to number our days. The prayer of Moses: our time is short, so let counting it make us wise. Today's word.
screen: `TEACH US TO NUMBER OUR DAYS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: number your days. Grass by evening, wisdom by morning. Day one hundred seventy-four, counted.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 89 [90] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, when the readings turn to the shortness of life.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy psalm about death.
what it means: a prayer of Moses that sets our short time beside God's long time and asks for wisdom.
what a scholar hears: the Hebrew says teach us to number our days; the Vulgate, and the Douay after it, read make thy right hand known. the old versions differ, and the sources do not settle why.

notes: Douay Psalm 89:1, 89:4 and 2 Peter 3:8 wording: confirm against a Challoner edition.

Psalm 90:12: Hebrew 'teach us to number our days'; Vulgate 'dexteram tuam sic notam fac, et eruditos corde in sapientia', Douay 'So make thy right hand known: and men learned in heart, in wisdom'. The script states the difference without explaining its cause.
'The oldest voice in the psalter, by tradition': the heading attributes it to Moses; hedged 'by tradition'.
